# flate2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/flate2/

## Expand description

A DEFLATE-based stream compression/decompression library

This library provides support for compression and decompression of DEFLATE-based streams:

- the DEFLATE format itself
- the zlib format
- gzip

These three formats are all closely related and largely only differ in their headers/footers. This crate has three types in each submodule for dealing with these three formats.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

In addition to supporting three formats, this crate supports several different
backends, controlled through this crate’s *features flags*:

-
`default`, or`rust_backend`- this implementation currently uses the`miniz_oxide`crate which is a port of`miniz.c`to Rust. This feature does not require a C compiler, and only uses safe Rust code.Note that the `rust_backend`feature may at some point be switched to use`zlib-rs`, and that`miniz_oxide`should be used explicitly if this is not desired.
-
`zlib-rs`- this implementation utilizes the`zlib-rs`crate, a Rust rewrite of zlib. This backend is the fastest, at the cost of some`unsafe`Rust code.

Several backends implemented in C are also available. These are useful in case you are already using a specific C implementation and need the result of compression to be bit-identical. See the crate’s README for details on the available C backends.

The `zlib-rs` backend typically outperforms all the C implementations.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

- `miniz_oxide`- *(enabled by default)*— This implementation uses only safe Rust code and doesn’t require a C compiler. It provides good performance for most use cases while being completely portable.
- `default`

[§](https://docs.rs#user-facing-backend-features)User-Facing Backend Features

Choose one of these features to select the compression backend.
Only one backend should be enabled at a time, or else one will see an unstable order which is currently
`zlib-ng`, `zlib-rs`, `cloudflare_zlib`, `miniz_oxide` and which may change at any time.

-
`rust_backend`*(enabled by default)*— Use the pure Rust`miniz_oxide`backend (default). This implementation uses only safe Rust code and doesn’t require a C compiler. It provides good performance for most use cases while being completely portable.Note that this feature at some point may be switched to use `zlib-rs`instead.
-
`zlib-rs``unsafe`code. It does not require a C compiler but uses`unsafe`Rust for optimization.
-
`miniz_oxide`*(enabled by default)*— Use the pure Rust`miniz_oxide`backend.
-
`zlib`
-
`zlib-default``zlib`but enables additional features from libz-sys.
-
`zlib-ng-compat``zlib-ng`feature. When using this feature, if any crate in your dependency graph explicitly requests stock zlib, or uses libz-sys directly without`default-features = false`, you’ll get stock zlib rather than zlib-ng. See[the libz-sys README](https://github.com/rust-lang/libz-sys/blob/main/README.md)for details. To avoid that, use the`"zlib-ng"`feature instead.
-
`zlib-ng`
-
`cloudflare_zlib`- ⚠ Does not support 32-bit CPUs and is incompatible with mingw.
- ⚠ May cause conflicts if other crates use different zlib versions.

-
`miniz-sys``rust_backend`, provided for backwards compatibility. Use`rust_backend`instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#internal-features)Internal Features

These features are used internally for backend selection and should not be enabled directly by users. They are documented here to aid with maintenance.

- `any_zlib`- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any zlib-based C backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by- `zlib-rs`,- `zlib`,- `zlib-ng`,- `zlib-ng-compat`, and- `cloudflare_zlib`. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.
- `any_c_zlib`- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any C based fully zlib compatible backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by- `zlib`,- `zlib-ng`,- `zlib-ng-compat`, and- `cloudflare_zlib`. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.
- `any_impl`- *(enabled by default)*—- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any compression backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by all backend features to ensure at least one implementation is available. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#ambiguous-feature-selection)Ambiguous feature selection

As Cargo features are additive, while backends are not, there is an order in which backends become active if multiple are selected.

- zlib-ng
- zlib-rs
- cloudflare_zlib
- miniz_oxide

[§](https://docs.rs#organization)Organization

This crate consists of three main modules: `bufread`, `read`, and `write`. Each module
implements DEFLATE, zlib, and gzip for [ std::io::BufRead](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.BufRead.html) input types,

[input types, and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)

`std::io::Read`[output types respectively.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`std::io::Write`Use the [ bufread](https://docs.rs/bufread/index.html) implementations if you can provide a

`BufRead` type for the input.
The `&[u8]` slice type implements the `BufRead` trait.The [ read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html) implementations conveniently wrap a

`Read` type in a `BufRead` implementation.
However, the `read` implementations may
[read past the end of the input data](https://github.com/rust-lang/flate2-rs/issues/338), making the

`Read` type useless for subsequent reads of the input. If you need to re-use the
`Read` type, wrap it in a [, use the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/buffered/bufreader/struct.BufReader.html)

`std::io::BufReader``bufread` implementations,
and perform subsequent reads on the `BufReader`.The [ write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html) implementations are most useful when there is no way to create a

`BufRead`
type, notably when reading async iterators (streams).```
use futures::{Stream, StreamExt};
use std::io::{Result, Write as _};
async fn decompress_gzip_stream<S, I>(stream: S) -> Result<Vec<u8>>
where
    S: Stream<Item = I>,
    I: AsRef<[u8]>
{
    let mut stream = std::pin::pin!(stream);
    let mut w = Vec::<u8>::new();
    let mut decoder = flate2::write::GzDecoder::new(w);
    while let Some(input) = stream.next().await {
        decoder.write_all(input.as_ref())?;
    }
    decoder.finish()
}
```
Note that types which operate over a specific trait often implement the mirroring trait as well.
For example a `bufread::DeflateDecoder<T>` *also* implements the
[ Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html) trait if

`T: Write`. That is, the “dual trait” is forwarded directly
to the underlying object if available.[§](https://docs.rs#about-multi-member-gzip-files)About multi-member Gzip files

While most `gzip` files one encounters will have a single *member* that can be read
with the [ GzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.GzDecoder.html), there may be some files which have multiple members.

A [ GzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.GzDecoder.html) will only read the first member of gzip data, which may unexpectedly
provide partial results when a multi-member gzip file is encountered.

`GzDecoder` is appropriate
for data that is designed to be read as single members from a multi-member file. `bufread::GzDecoder`
and `write::GzDecoder` also allow non-gzip data following gzip data to be handled.The [ MultiGzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.MultiGzDecoder.html) on the other hand will decode all members of a

`gzip` file
into one consecutive stream of bytes, which hides the underlying *members*entirely. If a file contains non-gzip data after the gzip data, MultiGzDecoder will emit an error after decoding the gzip data. This behavior matches the

`gzip`,
`gunzip`, and `zcat` command line tools.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [bufread](https://docs.rs/bufread/index.html)
- Types which operate over `BufRead`
- [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html)
- Types which operate over `Read`
- [write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html)
- Types which operate over `Write`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Compress](https://docs.rs/struct.Compress.html)
- Raw in-memory compression stream for blocks of data.
- [Compress](https://docs.rs/struct.CompressError.html)- Error
- Error returned when a compression object is used incorrectly or otherwise generates an error.
- [Compression](https://docs.rs/struct.Compression.html)
- When compressing data, the compression level can be specified by a value in this struct.
- [Crc](https://docs.rs/struct.Crc.html)- `zlib-rs`
- The CRC calculated by a `CrcReader`
- [CrcReader](https://docs.rs/struct.CrcReader.html)
- A wrapper around a `Read`
- [CrcWriter](https://docs.rs/struct.CrcWriter.html)
- A wrapper around a `Write`
- [Decompress](https://docs.rs/struct.Decompress.html)
- Raw in-memory decompression stream for blocks of data.
- [Decompress](https://docs.rs/struct.DecompressError.html)- Error
- Error returned when a decompression object finds that the input stream of bytes was not a valid input stream of bytes.
- [GzBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.GzBuilder.html)
- A builder structure to create a new gzip Encoder.
- [GzHeader](https://docs.rs/struct.GzHeader.html)
- A structure representing the header of a gzip stream.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Flush](https://docs.rs/enum.FlushCompress.html)- Compress
- Values which indicate the form of flushing to be used when compressing in-memory data.
- [Flush](https://docs.rs/enum.FlushDecompress.html)- Decompress
- Values which indicate the form of flushing to be used when decompressing in-memory data.
- [Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html)
- Possible status results of compressing some data or successfully decompressing a block of data.

---

# flate2 1.1.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/flate2/latest

# flate2

A streaming compression/decompression library DEFLATE-based streams in Rust.

This crate by default uses the `miniz_oxide` crate, a port of `miniz.c` to pure
Rust. This crate also supports other [backends](https://docs.rs#backends), such as the widely
available zlib library or the high-performance zlib-ng library.

Supported formats:

- deflate
- zlib
- gzip

```
# Cargo.toml
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## MSRV (Minimum Supported Rust Version) Policy

This crate supports the current and previous stable versions of the Rust compiler. For example, if the current stable is 1.80, this crate supports 1.80 and 1.79.

Other compiler versions may work, but failures may not be treated as a `flate2` bug.

The `Cargo.toml` file specifies a `rust-version` for which builds of the current version
passed at some point. This value is indicative only, and may change at any time.

The `rust-version` is a best-effort measured value and is different to the MSRV. The
`rust-version` can be incremented by a PR in order to pass tests, as long as the MSRV
continues to hold. When the `rust-version` increases, the next release should be a minor
version, to allow any affected users to pin to a previous minor version.

## Compression

```
use *;
use Compression;
use ZlibEncoder;
```
## Decompression

```
use *;
use GzDecoder;
```
## Backends

The default `miniz_oxide` backend has the advantage of only using safe Rust.

If you want maximum performance while still benefiting from a Rust
implementation at the cost of some `unsafe`, you can use `zlib-rs`:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0.17",  = ["zlib-rs"],  = false }
```
### C backends

While zlib-rs is [the fastest overall](https://trifectatech.org/blog/zlib-rs-is-faster-than-c/),
the zlib-ng C library can be slightly faster in certain cases:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0.17",  = ["zlib-ng"],  = false }
```
Note that the `"zlib-ng"` feature works even if some other part of your crate
graph depends on zlib.

However, if you're already using another C or Rust library that depends on zlib, and you want to avoid including both zlib and zlib-ng, you can use that for Rust code as well:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0.17",  = ["zlib"],  = false }
```
Or, if you have C or Rust code that depends on zlib and you want to use zlib-ng via libz-sys in zlib-compat mode, use:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0.17",  = ["zlib-ng-compat"],  = false }
```
Note that when using the `"zlib-ng-compat"` feature, if any crate in your
dependency graph explicitly requests stock zlib, or uses libz-sys directly
without `default-features = false`, you'll get stock zlib rather than zlib-ng.
See [the libz-sys
README](https://github.com/rust-lang/libz-sys/blob/main/README.md) for details.
To avoid that, use the `"zlib-ng"` feature instead.

For compatibility with previous versions of `flate2`, the Cloudflare optimized
version of zlib is available, via the `cloudflare_zlib` feature. It's not as
fast as zlib-ng, but it's faster than stock zlib. It requires an x86-64 CPU with
SSE 4.2 or ARM64 with NEON & CRC. It does not support 32-bit CPUs at all and is
incompatible with mingw. For more information check the [crate
documentation](https://crates.io/crates/cloudflare-zlib-sys). Note that
`cloudflare_zlib` will cause breakage if any other crate in your crate graph
uses another version of zlib/libz.

# flate2 1.1.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/flate2/latest/source/

DEFLATE compression and decompression exposed as Read/BufRead/Write streams.
Supports miniz_oxide and multiple zlib implementations. Supports zlib, gzip,
and raw deflate streams.

---

# cloudflare_zlib_sys - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cloudflare-zlib-sys/^0.3.6/

## Expand description

It requires x86-64 CPU with SSE 4.2 or ARM64 with NEON & CRC.

# miniz_oxide - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/miniz_oxide/^0.8.5/

## Expand description

A pure rust replacement for the [miniz](https://github.com/richgel999/miniz)
DEFLATE/zlib encoder/decoder.
Used a rust back-end for the
[flate2](https://github.com/alexcrichton/flate2-rs) crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#simple-compressiondecompression)Simple compression/decompression:

```
use miniz_oxide::inflate::decompress_to_vec;
use miniz_oxide::deflate::compress_to_vec;
fn roundtrip(data: &[u8]) {
    let compressed = compress_to_vec(data, 6);
    let decompressed = decompress_to_vec(compressed.as_slice()).expect("Failed to decompress!");
}
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [deflate](https://docs.rs/deflate/index.html)
- This module contains functionality for compression.
- [inflate](https://docs.rs/inflate/index.html)
- This module contains functionality for decompression.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamResult.html)- Result
- A structure containing the result of a call to the inflate or deflate streaming functions.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Data](https://docs.rs/enum.DataFormat.html)- Format
- How compressed data is wrapped.
- [MZError](https://docs.rs/enum.MZError.html)
- A list of miniz failed status codes.
- [MZFlush](https://docs.rs/enum.MZFlush.html)
- A list of flush types.
- [MZStatus](https://docs.rs/enum.MZStatus.html)
- A list of miniz successful status codes.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [MZResult](https://docs.rs/type.MZResult.html)
- `Result`alias for all miniz status codes both successful and failed.

# futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3/

## Expand description

Abstractions for asynchronous programming.

This crate provides a number of core abstractions for writing asynchronous code:

- [Futures](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)are single eventual values produced by asynchronous computations. Some programming languages (e.g. JavaScript) call this concept “promise”.
- [Streams](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)represent a series of values produced asynchronously.
- [Sinks](https://docs.rs/sink/index.html)provide support for asynchronous writing of data.
- [Executors](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html)are responsible for running asynchronous tasks.

The crate also contains abstractions for [asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) and
[cross-task communication](https://docs.rs/channel/index.html).

Underlying all of this is the *task system*, which is a form of lightweight
threading. Large asynchronous computations are built up using futures,
streams and sinks, and then spawned as independent tasks that are run to
completion, but *do not block* the thread running them.

The following example describes how the task system context is built and used within macros and keywords such as async and await!.

```
fn main() {
    let pool = ThreadPool::new().expect("Failed to build pool");
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::unbounded::<i32>();
    // Create a future by an async block, where async is responsible for an
    // implementation of Future. At this point no executor has been provided
    // to this future, so it will not be running.
    let fut_values = async {
        // Create another async block, again where the Future implementation
        // is generated by async. Since this is inside of a parent async block,
        // it will be provided with the executor of the parent block when the parent
        // block is executed.
        //
        // This executor chaining is done by Future::poll whose second argument
        // is a std::task::Context. This represents our executor, and the Future
        // implemented by this async block can be polled using the parent async
        // block's executor.
        let fut_tx_result = async move {
            (0..100).for_each(|v| {
                tx.unbounded_send(v).expect("Failed to send");
            })
        };
        // Use the provided thread pool to spawn the generated future
        // responsible for transmission
        pool.spawn_ok(fut_tx_result);
        let fut_values = rx
            .map(|v| v * 2)
            .collect();
        // Use the executor provided to this async block to wait for the
        // future to complete.
        fut_values.await
    };
    // Actually execute the above future, which will invoke Future::poll and
    // subsequently chain appropriate Future::poll and methods needing executors
    // to drive all futures. Eventually fut_values will be driven to completion.
    let values: Vec<i32> = executor::block_on(fut_values);
    println!("Values={:?}", values);
}
```
The majority of examples and code snippets in this crate assume that they are inside an async block as written above.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html)- `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, returning a tuple of all results once complete.
- [pending](https://docs.rs/macro.pending.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which yields to the event loop once.
- [pin_mut](https://docs.rs/macro.pin_mut.html)
- Pins a value on the stack.
- [poll](https://docs.rs/macro.poll.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which returns the result of polling a future once within the
current `async`context.
- [ready](https://docs.rs/macro.ready.html)
- Extracts the successful type of `Poll<T>`.
- [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html)- `async-await`and- `std`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. If multiple futures are ready,
one will be pseudo-randomly selected at runtime. Futures directly
passed to `select!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/macro.select_biased.html)- biased - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. Unlike `select!``select_biased!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/macro.stream_select.html)- select - `async-await`and- `std`
- Combines several streams, all producing the same `Item`type, into one stream. This is similar to`select_all`but does not require the streams to all be the same type. It also keeps the streams inline, and does not require`Box<dyn Stream>`s to be allocated. Streams passed to this macro must be`Unpin`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html)- join - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, resolving to a `Result`

# quickcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quickcheck/^1.0/

## Expand description

This crate is a port of
[Haskell’s QuickCheck](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/QuickCheck).

QuickCheck is a library for random testing of program properties. The programmer provides a specification of the program, in the form of properties which functions should satisfy, and QuickCheck then tests that the properties hold in a large number of randomly generated cases.

For detailed examples, please see the
[README](https://github.com/BurntSushi/quickcheck).

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

In general, this crate considers the `Arbitrary` implementations provided as
implementation details. Strategies may or may not change over time, which may
cause new test failures, presumably due to the discovery of new bugs due to a
new kind of witness being generated. These sorts of changes may happen in
semver compatible releases.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/macro.quickcheck.html)
- A macro for writing quickcheck tests.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Gen](https://docs.rs/struct.Gen.html)
- `Gen`represents a PRNG.
- [NoShrink](https://docs.rs/struct.NoShrink.html)
- Wrapper for disabling shrinking for an Arbitrary
- [Quick](https://docs.rs/struct.QuickCheck.html)- Check
- The main `QuickCheck`type for setting configuration and running`QuickCheck`.
- [Test](https://docs.rs/struct.TestResult.html)- Result
- Describes the status of a single instance of a test.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- `Arbitrary`describes types whose values can be randomly generated and shrunk.
- [Testable](https://docs.rs/trait.Testable.html)
- `Testable`describes types (e.g., a function) whose values can be tested.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [empty_](https://docs.rs/fn.empty_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with zero elements.
- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/fn.quickcheck.html)
- Convenience function for running `QuickCheck`.
- [single_](https://docs.rs/fn.single_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with a single element.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.9/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// The prelude import enables methods we use below, specifically
// Rng::random, Rng::sample, SliceRandom::shuffle and IndexedRandom::choose.
use rand::prelude::*;
// Get an RNG:
let mut rng = rand::rng();
// Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
println!("char: '{}'", rng.random::<char>());
// Try printing a random alphanumeric value instead!
println!("alpha: '{}'", rng.sample(rand::distr::Alphanumeric) as char);
// Generate and shuffle a sequence:
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
// And take a random pick (yes, we didn't need to shuffle first!):
let _ = nums.choose(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

- `pub use`- [rand_core](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html);

# flate2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/flate2/latest/target-redirect/flate2/

## Expand description

A DEFLATE-based stream compression/decompression library

This library provides support for compression and decompression of DEFLATE-based streams:

- the DEFLATE format itself
- the zlib format
- gzip

These three formats are all closely related and largely only differ in their headers/footers. This crate has three types in each submodule for dealing with these three formats.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

In addition to supporting three formats, this crate supports several different
backends, controlled through this crate’s *features flags*:

-
`default`, or`rust_backend`- this implementation currently uses the`miniz_oxide`crate which is a port of`miniz.c`to Rust. This feature does not require a C compiler, and only uses safe Rust code.Note that the `rust_backend`feature may at some point be switched to use`zlib-rs`, and that`miniz_oxide`should be used explicitly if this is not desired.
-
`zlib-rs`- this implementation utilizes the`zlib-rs`crate, a Rust rewrite of zlib. This backend is the fastest, at the cost of some`unsafe`Rust code.

Several backends implemented in C are also available. These are useful in case you are already using a specific C implementation and need the result of compression to be bit-identical. See the crate’s README for details on the available C backends.

The `zlib-rs` backend typically outperforms all the C implementations.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

- `miniz_oxide`- *(enabled by default)*— This implementation uses only safe Rust code and doesn’t require a C compiler. It provides good performance for most use cases while being completely portable.
- `default`

[§](https://docs.rs#user-facing-backend-features)User-Facing Backend Features

Choose one of these features to select the compression backend.
Only one backend should be enabled at a time, or else one will see an unstable order which is currently
`zlib-ng`, `zlib-rs`, `cloudflare_zlib`, `miniz_oxide` and which may change at any time.

-
`rust_backend`*(enabled by default)*— Use the pure Rust`miniz_oxide`backend (default). This implementation uses only safe Rust code and doesn’t require a C compiler. It provides good performance for most use cases while being completely portable.Note that this feature at some point may be switched to use `zlib-rs`instead.
-
`zlib-rs``unsafe`code. It does not require a C compiler but uses`unsafe`Rust for optimization.
-
`miniz_oxide`*(enabled by default)*— Use the pure Rust`miniz_oxide`backend.
-
`zlib`
-
`zlib-default``zlib`but enables additional features from libz-sys.
-
`zlib-ng-compat``zlib-ng`feature. When using this feature, if any crate in your dependency graph explicitly requests stock zlib, or uses libz-sys directly without`default-features = false`, you’ll get stock zlib rather than zlib-ng. See[the libz-sys README](https://github.com/rust-lang/libz-sys/blob/main/README.md)for details. To avoid that, use the`"zlib-ng"`feature instead.
-
`zlib-ng`
-
`cloudflare_zlib`- ⚠ Does not support 32-bit CPUs and is incompatible with mingw.
- ⚠ May cause conflicts if other crates use different zlib versions.

-
`miniz-sys``rust_backend`, provided for backwards compatibility. Use`rust_backend`instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#internal-features)Internal Features

These features are used internally for backend selection and should not be enabled directly by users. They are documented here to aid with maintenance.

- `any_zlib`- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any zlib-based C backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by- `zlib-rs`,- `zlib`,- `zlib-ng`,- `zlib-ng-compat`, and- `cloudflare_zlib`. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.
- `any_c_zlib`- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any C based fully zlib compatible backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by- `zlib`,- `zlib-ng`,- `zlib-ng-compat`, and- `cloudflare_zlib`. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.
- `any_impl`- *(enabled by default)*—- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any compression backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by all backend features to ensure at least one implementation is available. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#ambiguous-feature-selection)Ambiguous feature selection

As Cargo features are additive, while backends are not, there is an order in which backends become active if multiple are selected.

- zlib-ng
- zlib-rs
- cloudflare_zlib
- miniz_oxide

[§](https://docs.rs#organization)Organization

This crate consists of three main modules: `bufread`, `read`, and `write`. Each module
implements DEFLATE, zlib, and gzip for [ std::io::BufRead](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.BufRead.html) input types,

[input types, and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)

`std::io::Read`[output types respectively.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`std::io::Write`Use the [ bufread](https://docs.rs/bufread/index.html) implementations if you can provide a

`BufRead` type for the input.
The `&[u8]` slice type implements the `BufRead` trait.The [ read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html) implementations conveniently wrap a

`Read` type in a `BufRead` implementation.
However, the `read` implementations may
[read past the end of the input data](https://github.com/rust-lang/flate2-rs/issues/338), making the

`Read` type useless for subsequent reads of the input. If you need to re-use the
`Read` type, wrap it in a [, use the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/buffered/bufreader/struct.BufReader.html)

`std::io::BufReader``bufread` implementations,
and perform subsequent reads on the `BufReader`.The [ write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html) implementations are most useful when there is no way to create a

`BufRead`
type, notably when reading async iterators (streams).```
use futures::{Stream, StreamExt};
use std::io::{Result, Write as _};
async fn decompress_gzip_stream<S, I>(stream: S) -> Result<Vec<u8>>
where
    S: Stream<Item = I>,
    I: AsRef<[u8]>
{
    let mut stream = std::pin::pin!(stream);
    let mut w = Vec::<u8>::new();
    let mut decoder = flate2::write::GzDecoder::new(w);
    while let Some(input) = stream.next().await {
        decoder.write_all(input.as_ref())?;
    }
    decoder.finish()
}
```
Note that types which operate over a specific trait often implement the mirroring trait as well.
For example a `bufread::DeflateDecoder<T>` *also* implements the
[ Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html) trait if

`T: Write`. That is, the “dual trait” is forwarded directly
to the underlying object if available.[§](https://docs.rs#about-multi-member-gzip-files)About multi-member Gzip files

While most `gzip` files one encounters will have a single *member* that can be read
with the [ GzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.GzDecoder.html), there may be some files which have multiple members.

A [ GzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.GzDecoder.html) will only read the first member of gzip data, which may unexpectedly
provide partial results when a multi-member gzip file is encountered.

`GzDecoder` is appropriate
for data that is designed to be read as single members from a multi-member file. `bufread::GzDecoder`
and `write::GzDecoder` also allow non-gzip data following gzip data to be handled.The [ MultiGzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.MultiGzDecoder.html) on the other hand will decode all members of a

`gzip` file
into one consecutive stream of bytes, which hides the underlying *members*entirely. If a file contains non-gzip data after the gzip data, MultiGzDecoder will emit an error after decoding the gzip data. This behavior matches the

`gzip`,
`gunzip`, and `zcat` command line tools.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [bufread](https://docs.rs/bufread/index.html)
- Types which operate over `BufRead`
- [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html)
- Types which operate over `Read`
- [write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html)
- Types which operate over `Write`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Compress](https://docs.rs/struct.Compress.html)
- Raw in-memory compression stream for blocks of data.
- [Compress](https://docs.rs/struct.CompressError.html)- Error
- Error returned when a compression object is used incorrectly or otherwise generates an error.

- A wrapper around a `Read`
- [CrcWriter](https://docs.rs/struct.CrcWriter.html)
- A wrapper around a `Write`
- [Decompress](https://docs.rs/struct.Decompress.html)
- Raw in-memory decompression stream for blocks of data.
- [Decompress](https://docs.rs/struct.DecompressError.html)- Error
- Error returned when a decompression object finds that the input stream of bytes was not a valid input stream of bytes.
- [GzBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.GzBuilder.html)
- A builder structure to create a new gzip Encoder.
- [GzHeader](https://docs.rs/struct.GzHeader.html)
- A structure representing the header of a gzip stream.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

                                    actr-runtime-mailbox 0.4.8
                                ](https://docs.rs/crate/actr-runtime-mailbox/0.4.8/builds) | 8s | 26s |

# flate2 1.1.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/flate2/1.1.9

# flate2

A streaming compression/decompression library DEFLATE-based streams in Rust.

This crate by default uses the `miniz_oxide` crate, a port of `miniz.c` to pure
Rust. This crate also supports other [backends](https://docs.rs#backends), such as the widely
available zlib library or the high-performance zlib-ng library.

Supported formats:

- deflate
- zlib
- gzip

```
# Cargo.toml
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## MSRV (Minimum Supported Rust Version) Policy

This crate supports the current and previous stable versions of the Rust compiler. For example, if the current stable is 1.80, this crate supports 1.80 and 1.79.

Other compiler versions may work, but failures may not be treated as a `flate2` bug.

The `Cargo.toml` file specifies a `rust-version` for which builds of the current version
passed at some point. This value is indicative only, and may change at any time.

The `rust-version` is a best-effort measured value and is different to the MSRV. The
`rust-version` can be incremented by a PR in order to pass tests, as long as the MSRV
continues to hold. When the `rust-version` increases, the next release should be a minor
version, to allow any affected users to pin to a previous minor version.

## Compression

```
use *;
use Compression;
use ZlibEncoder;
```
## Decompression

```
use *;
use GzDecoder;
```
## Backends

The default `miniz_oxide` backend has the advantage of only using safe Rust.

If you want maximum performance while still benefiting from a Rust
implementation at the cost of some `unsafe`, you can use `zlib-rs`:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0.17",  = ["zlib-rs"],  = false }
```
### C backends

While zlib-rs is [the fastest overall](https://trifectatech.org/blog/zlib-rs-is-faster-than-c/),
the zlib-ng C library can be slightly faster in certain cases:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0.17",  = ["zlib-ng"],  = false }
```
Note that the `"zlib-ng"` feature works even if some other part of your crate
graph depends on zlib.

However, if you're already using another C or Rust library that depends on zlib, and you want to avoid including both zlib and zlib-ng, you can use that for Rust code as well:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0.17",  = ["zlib"],  = false }
```
Or, if you have C or Rust code that depends on zlib and you want to use zlib-ng via libz-sys in zlib-compat mode, use:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0.17",  = ["zlib-ng-compat"],  = false }
```
Note that when using the `"zlib-ng-compat"` feature, if any crate in your
dependency graph explicitly requests stock zlib, or uses libz-sys directly
without `default-features = false`, you'll get stock zlib rather than zlib-ng.
See [the libz-sys
README](https://github.com/rust-lang/libz-sys/blob/main/README.md) for details.
To avoid that, use the `"zlib-ng"` feature instead.

For compatibility with previous versions of `flate2`, the Cloudflare optimized
version of zlib is available, via the `cloudflare_zlib` feature. It's not as
fast as zlib-ng, but it's faster than stock zlib. It requires an x86-64 CPU with
SSE 4.2 or ARM64 with NEON & CRC. It does not support 32-bit CPUs at all and is
incompatible with mingw. For more information check the [crate
documentation](https://crates.io/crates/cloudflare-zlib-sys). Note that
`cloudflare_zlib` will cause breakage if any other crate in your crate graph
uses another version of zlib/libz.

# License

- Apache License, Version 2.0, ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in this project by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# flate2 1.1.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/flate2/1.1.9/source/

DEFLATE compression and decompression exposed as Read/BufRead/Write streams.
Supports miniz_oxide and multiple zlib implementations. Supports zlib, gzip,
and raw deflate streams.

---

# flate2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/flate2/1.1.9/target-redirect/flate2/

## Expand description

A DEFLATE-based stream compression/decompression library

This library provides support for compression and decompression of DEFLATE-based streams:

- the DEFLATE format itself
- the zlib format
- gzip

These three formats are all closely related and largely only differ in their headers/footers. This crate has three types in each submodule for dealing with these three formats.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

In addition to supporting three formats, this crate supports several different
backends, controlled through this crate’s *features flags*:

-
`default`, or`rust_backend`- this implementation currently uses the`miniz_oxide`crate which is a port of`miniz.c`to Rust. This feature does not require a C compiler, and only uses safe Rust code.Note that the `rust_backend`feature may at some point be switched to use`zlib-rs`, and that`miniz_oxide`should be used explicitly if this is not desired.
-
`zlib-rs`- this implementation utilizes the`zlib-rs`crate, a Rust rewrite of zlib. This backend is the fastest, at the cost of some`unsafe`Rust code.

Several backends implemented in C are also available. These are useful in case you are already using a specific C implementation and need the result of compression to be bit-identical. See the crate’s README for details on the available C backends.

The `zlib-rs` backend typically outperforms all the C implementations.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

- `miniz_oxide`- *(enabled by default)*— This implementation uses only safe Rust code and doesn’t require a C compiler. It provides good performance for most use cases while being completely portable.
- `default`

[§](https://docs.rs#user-facing-backend-features)User-Facing Backend Features

Choose one of these features to select the compression backend.
Only one backend should be enabled at a time, or else one will see an unstable order which is currently
`zlib-ng`, `zlib-rs`, `cloudflare_zlib`, `miniz_oxide` and which may change at any time.

-
`rust_backend`*(enabled by default)*— Use the pure Rust`miniz_oxide`backend (default). This implementation uses only safe Rust code and doesn’t require a C compiler. It provides good performance for most use cases while being completely portable.Note that this feature at some point may be switched to use `zlib-rs`instead.
-
`zlib-rs``unsafe`code. It does not require a C compiler but uses`unsafe`Rust for optimization.
-
`miniz_oxide`*(enabled by default)*— Use the pure Rust`miniz_oxide`backend.
-
`zlib`
-
`zlib-default``zlib`but enables additional features from libz-sys.
-
`zlib-ng-compat``zlib-ng`feature. When using this feature, if any crate in your dependency graph explicitly requests stock zlib, or uses libz-sys directly without`default-features = false`, you’ll get stock zlib rather than zlib-ng. See[the libz-sys README](https://github.com/rust-lang/libz-sys/blob/main/README.md)for details. To avoid that, use the`"zlib-ng"`feature instead.
-
`zlib-ng`
-
`cloudflare_zlib`- ⚠ Does not support 32-bit CPUs and is incompatible with mingw.
- ⚠ May cause conflicts if other crates use different zlib versions.

-
`miniz-sys``rust_backend`, provided for backwards compatibility. Use`rust_backend`instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#internal-features)Internal Features

These features are used internally for backend selection and should not be enabled directly by users. They are documented here to aid with maintenance.

- `any_zlib`- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any zlib-based C backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by- `zlib-rs`,- `zlib`,- `zlib-ng`,- `zlib-ng-compat`, and- `cloudflare_zlib`. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.
- `any_c_zlib`- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any C based fully zlib compatible backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by- `zlib`,- `zlib-ng`,- `zlib-ng-compat`, and- `cloudflare_zlib`. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.
- `any_impl`- *(enabled by default)*—- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any compression backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by all backend features to ensure at least one implementation is available. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#ambiguous-feature-selection)Ambiguous feature selection

As Cargo features are additive, while backends are not, there is an order in which backends become active if multiple are selected.

- zlib-ng
- zlib-rs
- cloudflare_zlib
- miniz_oxide

[§](https://docs.rs#organization)Organization

This crate consists of three main modules: `bufread`, `read`, and `write`. Each module
implements DEFLATE, zlib, and gzip for [ std::io::BufRead](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.BufRead.html) input types,

[input types, and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)

`std::io::Read`[output types respectively.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`std::io::Write`Use the [ bufread](https://docs.rs/bufread/index.html) implementations if you can provide a

`BufRead` type for the input.
The `&[u8]` slice type implements the `BufRead` trait.The [ read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html) implementations conveniently wrap a

`Read` type in a `BufRead` implementation.
However, the `read` implementations may
[read past the end of the input data](https://github.com/rust-lang/flate2-rs/issues/338), making the

`Read` type useless for subsequent reads of the input. If you need to re-use the
`Read` type, wrap it in a [, use the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/buffered/bufreader/struct.BufReader.html)

`std::io::BufReader``bufread` implementations,
and perform subsequent reads on the `BufReader`.The [ write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html) implementations are most useful when there is no way to create a

`BufRead`
type, notably when reading async iterators (streams).```
use futures::{Stream, StreamExt};
use std::io::{Result, Write as _};
async fn decompress_gzip_stream<S, I>(stream: S) -> Result<Vec<u8>>
where
    S: Stream<Item = I>,
    I: AsRef<[u8]>
{
    let mut stream = std::pin::pin!(stream);
    let mut w = Vec::<u8>::new();
    let mut decoder = flate2::write::GzDecoder::new(w);
    while let Some(input) = stream.next().await {
        decoder.write_all(input.as_ref())?;
    }
    decoder.finish()
}
```
Note that types which operate over a specific trait often implement the mirroring trait as well.
For example a `bufread::DeflateDecoder<T>` *also* implements the
[ Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html) trait if

`T: Write`. That is, the “dual trait” is forwarded directly
to the underlying object if available.[§](https://docs.rs#about-multi-member-gzip-files)About multi-member Gzip files

While most `gzip` files one encounters will have a single *member* that can be read
with the [ GzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.GzDecoder.html), there may be some files which have multiple members.

A [ GzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.GzDecoder.html) will only read the first member of gzip data, which may unexpectedly
provide partial results when a multi-member gzip file is encountered.

`GzDecoder` is appropriate
for data that is designed to be read as single members from a multi-member file. `bufread::GzDecoder`
and `write::GzDecoder` also allow non-gzip data following gzip data to be handled.The [ MultiGzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.MultiGzDecoder.html) on the other hand will decode all members of a

`gzip` file
into one consecutive stream of bytes, which hides the underlying *members*entirely. If a file contains non-gzip data after the gzip data, MultiGzDecoder will emit an error after decoding the gzip data. This behavior matches the

`gzip`,
`gunzip`, and `zcat` command line tools.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [bufread](https://docs.rs/bufread/index.html)
- Types which operate over `BufRead`
- [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html)
- Types which operate over `Read`
- [write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html)
- Types which operate over `Write`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Compress](https://docs.rs/struct.Compress.html)
- Raw in-memory compression stream for blocks of data.
- [Compress](https://docs.rs/struct.CompressError.html)- Error
- Error returned when a compression object is used incorrectly or otherwise generates an error.
- [Compression](https://docs.rs/struct.Compression.html)
- When compressing data, the compression level can be specified by a value in this struct.
- [Crc](https://docs.rs/struct.Crc.html)- `zlib-rs`
- The CRC calculated by a `CrcReader`
- [CrcReader](https://docs.rs/struct.CrcReader.html)
- A wrapper around a `Read`
- [CrcWriter](https://docs.rs/struct.CrcWriter.html)
- A wrapper around a `Write`
- [Decompress](https://docs.rs/struct.Decompress.html)
- Raw in-memory decompression stream for blocks of data.
- [Decompress](https://docs.rs/struct.DecompressError.html)- Error
- Error returned when a decompression object finds that the input stream of bytes was not a valid input stream of bytes.
- [GzBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.GzBuilder.html)
- A builder structure to create a new gzip Encoder.
- [GzHeader](https://docs.rs/struct.GzHeader.html)
- A structure representing the header of a gzip stream.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Flush](https://docs.rs/enum.FlushCompress.html)- Compress
- Values which indicate the form of flushing to be used when compressing in-memory data.
- [Flush](https://docs.rs/enum.FlushDecompress.html)- Decompress
- Values which indicate the form of flushing to be used when decompressing in-memory data.
- [Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html)
- Possible status results of compressing some data or successfully decompressing a block of data.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/flate2/1.1.9/src/flate2/lib.rs.html

# flate2/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! A DEFLATE-based stream compression/decompression library
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! This library provides support for compression and decompression of
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! DEFLATE-based streams:
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! * the DEFLATE format itself
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! * the zlib format
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! * gzip
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! These three formats are all closely related and largely only differ in their
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! headers/footers. This crate has three types in each submodule for dealing
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! with these three formats.
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! # Implementation
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! In addition to supporting three formats, this crate supports several different
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! backends, controlled through this crate's *features flags*:
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! * `default`, or `rust_backend` - this implementation currently uses the `miniz_oxide`
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!   crate which is a port of `miniz.c` to Rust. This feature does not
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!   require a C compiler, and only uses safe Rust code.
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!   Note that the `rust_backend` feature may at some point be switched to use `zlib-rs`,
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!   and that `miniz_oxide` should be used explicitly if this is not desired.
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! * `zlib-rs` - this implementation utilizes the `zlib-rs` crate, a Rust rewrite of zlib.
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!   This backend is the fastest, at the cost of some `unsafe` Rust code.
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! Several backends implemented in C are also available.
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! These are useful in case you are already using a specific C implementation
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! and need the result of compression to be bit-identical.
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! See the crate's README for details on the available C backends.
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! The `zlib-rs` backend typically outperforms all the C implementations.
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! # Feature Flags
[37](https://docs.rs#37)#![cfg_attr(
[38](https://docs.rs#38)    not(feature = "document-features"),
[39](https://docs.rs#39)    doc = "Activate the `document-features` cargo feature to see feature docs here"
[40](https://docs.rs#40))]
[41](https://docs.rs#41)#![cfg_attr(feature = "document-features", doc = document_features::document_features!())]
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! ## Ambiguous feature selection
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! As Cargo features are additive, while backends are not, there is an order in which backends
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! become active if multiple are selected.
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! * zlib-ng
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! * zlib-rs
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! * cloudflare_zlib
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! * miniz_oxide
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! # Organization
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! This crate consists of three main modules: `bufread`, `read`, and `write`. Each module
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! implements DEFLATE, zlib, and gzip for [`std::io::BufRead`] input types, [`std::io::Read`] input
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! types, and [`std::io::Write`] output types respectively.
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! Use the [`mod@bufread`] implementations if you can provide a `BufRead` type for the input.
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! The `&[u8]` slice type implements the `BufRead` trait.
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! The [`mod@read`] implementations conveniently wrap a `Read` type in a `BufRead` implementation.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! However, the `read` implementations may
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! [read past the end of the input data](https://github.com/rust-lang/flate2-rs/issues/338),
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! making the `Read` type useless for subsequent reads of the input. If you need to re-use the
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! `Read` type, wrap it in a [`std::io::BufReader`], use the `bufread` implementations,
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! and perform subsequent reads on the `BufReader`.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! The [`mod@write`] implementations are most useful when there is no way to create a `BufRead`
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! type, notably when reading async iterators (streams).
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! ```
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! use futures::{Stream, StreamExt};
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! use std::io::{Result, Write as _};
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! async fn decompress_gzip_stream<S, I>(stream: S) -> Result<Vec<u8>>
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! where
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!     S: Stream<Item = I>,
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!     I: AsRef<[u8]>
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! {
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!     let mut stream = std::pin::pin!(stream);
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//!     let mut w = Vec::<u8>::new();
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!     let mut decoder = flate2::write::GzDecoder::new(w);
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!     while let Some(input) = stream.next().await {
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!         decoder.write_all(input.as_ref())?;
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!     }
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!     decoder.finish()
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! }
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! ```
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! Note that types which operate over a specific trait often implement the mirroring trait as well.
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! For example a `bufread::DeflateDecoder<T>` *also* implements the
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! [`Write`] trait if `T: Write`. That is, the "dual trait" is forwarded directly
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! to the underlying object if available.
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! # About multi-member Gzip files
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! While most `gzip` files one encounters will have a single *member* that can be read
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! with the [`GzDecoder`], there may be some files which have multiple members.
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! A [`GzDecoder`] will only read the first member of gzip data, which may unexpectedly
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! provide partial results when a multi-member gzip file is encountered. `GzDecoder` is appropriate
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! for data that is designed to be read as single members from a multi-member file. `bufread::GzDecoder`
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! and `write::GzDecoder` also allow non-gzip data following gzip data to be handled.
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! The [`MultiGzDecoder`] on the other hand will decode all members of a `gzip` file
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! into one consecutive stream of bytes, which hides the underlying *members* entirely.
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! If a file contains non-gzip data after the gzip data, MultiGzDecoder will
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! emit an error after decoding the gzip data. This behavior matches the `gzip`,
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! `gunzip`, and `zcat` command line tools.
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! [`Bufread`]: std::io::BufRead
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! [`BufReader`]: std::io::BufReader
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! [`Read`]: std::io::Read
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! [`Write`]: std::io::Write
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! [`GzDecoder`]: bufread::GzDecoder
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! [`MultiGzDecoder`]: bufread::MultiGzDecoder

# GzDecoder in flate2::bufread - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/flate2/1.1.9/flate2/bufread/struct.GzDecoder.html

Struct GzDecoder  Copy item path  Source  `pub struct GzDecoder<R> {  }`Expand description A decoder for a single member of a gzip file .

This structure implements a `Read``BufRead`

After reading a single member of the gzip data this reader will return
Ok(0) even if there are more bytes available in the underlying reader.
If you need the following bytes, call `into_inner()` after Ok(0) to
recover the underlying reader.

To handle gzip files that may have multiple members, see `MultiGzDecoder`in the introduction .

   let  mut  s = String::new();
   gz.read_to_string(&mut  s)? ;
   Ok (s)

# MultiGzDecoder in flate2::bufread - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/flate2/1.1.9/flate2/bufread/struct.MultiGzDecoder.html

`pub struct MultiGzDecoder<R>(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

A gzip streaming decoder that decodes a [gzip file](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1952#page-5) that may have multiple members.

This structure implements a [ Read](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Read.html) interface. When read from, it reads
compressed data from the underlying

[and provides the uncompressed data.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.BufRead.html)

`BufRead`A gzip file consists of a series of *members* concatenated one after another.
MultiGzDecoder decodes all members from the data and only returns Ok(0) when the
underlying reader does. For a file, this reads to the end of the file.

To handle members separately, see [GzDecoder](https://docs.rs/struct.GzDecoder.html) or read more
[in the introduction](https://docs.rs/index.html#about-multi-member-gzip-files).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::io::prelude::*;
use std::io;
use flate2::bufread::MultiGzDecoder;
// Uncompresses a Gz Encoded vector of bytes and returns a string or error
// Here &[u8] implements BufRead
fn decode_reader(bytes: Vec<u8>) -> io::Result<String> {
   let mut gz = MultiGzDecoder::new(&bytes[..]);
   let mut s = String::new();
   gz.read_to_string(&mut s)?;
   Ok(s)
}
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/flate2/gz/bufread.rs.html#397-404)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-MultiGzDecoder%3CR%3E)### impl<R: [BufRead](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.BufRead.html)> [MultiGzDecoder](https://docs.rs/struct.MultiGzDecoder.html)<R>

# Compress in flate2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/flate2/1.1.9/flate2/struct.Compress.html

`pub struct Compress { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Raw in-memory compression stream for blocks of data.

This type is the building block for the I/O streams in the rest of this
crate. It requires more management than the [ Read](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Read.html)/

[API but is maximally flexible in terms of accepting input from any source and being able to produce output to any memory location.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`Write`It is recommended to use the I/O stream adaptors over this type as they’re easier to use.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

) -> [Compress](https://docs.rs/struct.Compress.html)

**crate feature**only.

`any_zlib`Creates a new object ready for compressing data that it’s given.

The `level` argument here indicates what level of compression is going
to be performed, and the `zlib_header` argument indicates whether the
output data should have a zlib header or not. The `window_bits` parameter
indicates the base-2 logarithm of the sliding window size and must be
between 9 and 15.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

If `window_bits` does not fall into the range 9 ..= 15,
this function will panic.

**crate feature**only.

`any_zlib`Creates a new object ready for compressing data that it’s given.

The `level` argument here indicates what level of compression is going
to be performed.

The Compress object produced by this constructor outputs gzip headers for the compressed data.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

If `window_bits` does not fall into the range 9 ..= 15,
this function will panic.

Returns the total number of input bytes which have been processed by this compression object.

Returns the total number of output bytes which have been produced by this compression object.

This is equivalent to dropping this object and then creating a new one.

#### pub fn [set_level](https://docs.rs#method.set_level)(&mut self, level: [Compression](https://docs.rs/struct.Compression.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [CompressError](https://docs.rs/struct.CompressError.html)>

**crate feature**only.

`any_zlib`Dynamically updates the compression level.

This can be used to switch between compression levels for different kinds of data, or it can be used in conjunction with a call to reset to reuse the compressor.

This may return an error if there wasn’t enough output space to complete the compression of the available input data before changing the compression level. Flushing the stream before calling this method ensures that the function will succeed on the first call.

    input: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],

Compresses the input data into the output, consuming only as much input as needed and writing as much output as possible.

The flush option can be any of the available `FlushCompress` parameters.

To learn how much data was consumed or how much output was produced, use
the `total_in` and `total_out` functions before/after this is called.

#### pub fn [compress_vec](https://docs.rs#method.compress_vec)(
    &mut self,
    input: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
    output: &mut [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)>,
    flush: [FlushCompress](https://docs.rs/enum.FlushCompress.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html), [CompressError](https://docs.rs/struct.CompressError.html)>

Compresses the input data into the extra space of the output, consuming only as much input as needed and writing as much output as possible.

This function has the same semantics as `compress`, except that the
length of `vec` is managed by this function. This will not reallocate
the vector provided or attempt to grow it, so space for the output must
be reserved in the output vector by the caller before calling this
function.

# Compression in flate2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/flate2/1.1.9/flate2/struct.Compression.html

`pub struct Compression(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

When compressing data, the compression level can be specified by a value in this struct.

Creates a new description of the compression level with an explicitly specified integer.

The integer here is typically on a scale of 0-9 where 0 means “no compression” and 9 means “take as long as you’d like”.

# Decompress in flate2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/flate2/1.1.9/flate2/struct.Decompress.html

`pub struct Decompress { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Raw in-memory decompression stream for blocks of data.

This type is the building block for the I/O streams in the rest of this
crate. It requires more management than the [ Read](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Read.html)/

[API but is maximally flexible in terms of accepting input from any source and being able to produce output to any memory location.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`Write`It is recommended to use the I/O stream adaptors over this type as they’re easier to use.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/flate2/mem.rs.html#484-491)#### pub fn [decompress](https://docs.rs#method.decompress)(
    &mut self,
    input: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
    output: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
    flush: [FlushDecompress](https://docs.rs/enum.FlushDecompress.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html), [DecompressError](https://docs.rs/struct.DecompressError.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/flate2/mem.rs.html#484-491)

#### pub fn [decompress](https://docs.rs#method.decompress)(
    &mut self,
    input: &[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
    output: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)],
    flush: [FlushDecompress](https://docs.rs/enum.FlushDecompress.html),
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html), [DecompressError](https://docs.rs/struct.DecompressError.html)>

Decompresses the input data into the output, consuming only as much input as needed and writing as much output as possible.

The flush option can be any of the available `FlushDecompress` parameters.

If the first call passes `FlushDecompress::Finish` it is assumed that
the input and output buffers are both sized large enough to decompress
the entire stream in a single call.

A flush value of `FlushDecompress::Finish` indicates that there are no
more source bytes available beside what’s already in the input buffer,
and the output buffer is large enough to hold the rest of the
decompressed data.

To learn how much data was consumed or how much output was produced, use
the `total_in` and `total_out` functions before/after this is called.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

If the input data to this instance of `Decompress` is not a valid
zlib/deflate stream then this function may return an instance of
`DecompressError` to indicate that the stream of input bytes is corrupted.

) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html), [DecompressError](https://docs.rs/struct.DecompressError.html)>

Decompresses the input data into the extra space in the output vector
specified by `output`.

This function has the same semantics as `decompress`, except that the
length of `vec` is managed by this function. This will not reallocate
the vector provided or attempt to grow it, so space for the output must
be reserved in the output vector by the caller before calling this
function.

# GzBuilder in flate2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/flate2/1.1.9/flate2/struct.GzBuilder.html

`pub struct GzBuilder { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A builder structure to create a new gzip Encoder.

This structure controls header configuration options such as the filename.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::io::prelude::*;
use std::fs::File;
use flate2::GzBuilder;
use flate2::Compression;
// GzBuilder opens a file and writes a sample string using GzBuilder pattern
let f = File::create("examples/hello_world.gz")?;
let mut gz = GzBuilder::new()
                .filename("hello_world.txt")
                .comment("test file, please delete")
                .write(f, Compression::default());
gz.write_all(b"hello world")?;
gz.finish()?;
```
